turns.t: [warmly] Good morning, Singapore — it's Monday, the seventh of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three things before we start. The Gulf war is back on the water — America and Iran are sinking each other's tankers, and oil barely blinked.
[curious] The Fed's about to make a genuine coin-toss call — and gold is climbing like it doesn't care which way it goes.
And later, gravel cycling: the sport that sold itself as an escape and grew a twelve-thousand-dollar arms race.
[amused] Of course it did. Every escape gets a price tag eventually. Start with the Gulf.
So. For about a month, the Strait of Hormuz had gone quiet. That ended on Saturday.
What happened?
America struck three Iranian oil tankers — in reprisal, not just enforcing a blockade. Iran hit back: three tankers, three American-linked ships, and a ballistic missile fired toward US warships.
[thoughtful] Toward the carriers?
That's the Al Jazeera reporting — single-sourced, so hold it lightly. But the doctrine is the real shift. The White House approved what the coverage calls, quote, tanker for tanker.
Meaning America now sinks an Iranian tanker every time Iran hits shipping.
Exactly. And Tehran says it'll declare a restricted zone outside the Strait in the coming days — any ship that enters goes on a sanctions list.
[thoughtful] Okay, so here's what I don't get. That sounds like the start of an oil shock. What did crude actually do?
Brent settled at ninety-five dollars and four cents. Up eight, nine per cent on the week — but nowhere near March's one hundred twenty-six, and miles from the two-hundred-dollar doomcasts.
Why so calm?

China. It draws nearly two-fifths of its oil through that Strait, and it spent the summer cutting Iranian imports and building a months-long buffer. It's absorbing the shock, not confronting it. And about forty ships a day still transit — under American escort.
And the read from the different capitals?

Depends where you stand. Doha frames a months-long tanker war and calls Iran targeting the carriers a calculated escalation. Washington calls the very same doctrine calibrated deterrence — a US official says the earlier strikes bought at least a month of quiet. And the Beijing lens simply watches China absorb the shock.
[wry] So the war is real, the escalation is real, and the market has simply decided to believe both sides that it stays bounded.
That's the whole issue in one line, honestly. We called the spine this Monday the hold. Everyone's holding a position past the point of comfort.
And what breaks the calm? What's the number to watch?
An actually closed strait. A hit carrier. Or a strike on Iran's hardened nuclear sites. Short of that, it's a contained attrition war — and the bear case, weirdly, is boredom, not catastrophe.
[exhales] Right. There's a Ukraine piece too?
Brief one. Witkoff and Kushner saw Putin in Moscow on Friday, Zelensky in Kyiv on Saturday. The one concrete result: a three-day promise not to strike each other's capitals.
[deadpan] Three days.
Three days. The Kremlin called it constructive. Both sides said, quote, ideas. Nobody said terms.
[sighs] The smallest promise two governments can make. Let's do the money, because this is where the hold really lives.
The Fed. American jobs in August came in at a hundred sixty-two thousand — about three times what economists expected.
Strong.

Strong enough to flip the rate debate. Hike odds for the fifteenth-to-sixteenth meeting went from thirty per cent, to sixty-six after the chair's hawkish Jackson Hole, back to fifty when a governor pushed back, and settled near sixty after the jobs number.
[laughs] That's not a forecast, that's a heart monitor.
[deadpan] It's a coin-toss with a press conference. The real hinge is the inflation print on the eleventh — four days before they decide. A cool number and the hold survives; a hot one and they hike.
And the reader's portfolio — the all-world fund, global bonds, gold, bitcoin. Give me the read.

Rates are the dominant force. Firm real yields — the ten-year at four point seven nine per cent, the thirty-year above five — a firmer dollar, and that caps equities and weighs on bitcoin, which is soft around seventy-nine thousand seven hundred dollars.
And bonds?
Duration is the enemy in a higher-for-longer world. A four-per-cent coupon buys you income while the price erodes — and the equity-and-bond hedge is working less well than the screens suggest.
But gold's the strange one.
Gold is the odd one out. Four thousand four hundred seventy-six dollars — climbing into rising real yields, which normally crush it.
[curious] So what's holding it up?

Not rates at all. Geopolitics, central-bank buying, and a debt-and-debasement hedge. When gold rises against high real yields, that's the tell it's pricing something other than the Fed. And to be clear — this is analysis, not advice.
[thoughtful] So near record highs, but for a nervous reason.

Exactly. The all-world fund is near its high, but it's being tested, not confirmed — a hike plus firm real yields raises the discount rate on every future dollar of earnings. Resilience under pressure, not a green light.
Singapore's in the same story, isn't it? The growth call.
The forecasters lifted Singapore's twenty twenty-six growth to five per cent — up from three and a half in June. On the export boom.
[skeptical] Let me guess. The export boom is chips.
AI-linked hardware, yes. And here's the tell: nearly a third of those same forecasters named a bursting AI bubble as the top risk to the number they just raised.
[laughs] So they upgraded the forecast and pre-wrote its obituary in the same survey.
Which is our quote today. Upton Sinclair: it's difficult to get a man to understand something when his salary depends on his not understanding it.
[chuckles] Perfect. Also on the island — the haze.

Eased over the weekend. The reading crossed one hundred for the first time since twenty twenty-three, peaked around one hundred twenty-three overnight, then dropped — on the wind, not the diplomacy. The fires are still burning.
Good to know. Technology — big week for the labs.
The densest of the year. OpenAI shipped GPT-six Astra — the first model it says crossed its own critical-cyber threshold. Same seventy-two hours as new frontier models from Google and Anthropic.
[thoughtful] Wait — they're marketing the safety limit as a feature?
That's the sceptic's point exactly. Calling it the most cyber-capable model ever is a safety disclosure and a sales pitch in one breath — months after their own partner, Hugging Face, was breached.
Speaking of which — didn't Nvidia just buy Hugging Face?

Signed. Two September. Twelve point nine billion dollars, closing in the first half of twenty twenty-seven. And separately, Nvidia's funding a MediaTek deal that lists in Singapore tomorrow — which every analyst calls circular financing.
[thoughtful] It's the whole week in one shape, isn't it. The vendor funding its own customers, the model graded on a benchmark it wrote itself, the safeguard sold as the feature.
That's the hold in silicon. A trade held up by everyone who's paid to hold it — and Singapore's five-per-cent growth call is riding the same wave, which is why its own forecasters are nervous.
[amused] Nvidia funds the customers who buy Nvidia. Bold.

For the home lab: the open weights everyone wanted, GLM five point three, finally dropped after a two-week safety hold. But it's a cluster-sized model. On a single card, the pick is still Qwen three point eight, twenty-seven billion.
And the bad news for anyone building a rig?
Memory. The tabletop AI box jumped to four thousand six hundred ninety-nine dollars, and graphics-card street prices are up thirty-nine per cent since June. If you can wait, wait.
Now — the maker of the day. The Atelier did pocket knives, and I did not expect to be interested.
[wry] Nobody does, until they learn to read one. A folding knife is four systems: the steel, the lock, the handle, the pivot. Judge those and you can price any knife cold.
Give me the one thing to know about the steel.
A steel called MagnaCut. For decades every blade steel was a trade-off — sharpness against toughness against rust. MagnaCut broke that triangle. Chris Reeve moved its whole line to it.
[curious] And the buy-once pick?

The sweet spot is a Benchmade Bugout at a hundred eighty dollars, or a Spyderco at around two hundred. The grail is a Chris Reeve Sebenza at four-fifty to five-thirty — but honestly, that's finish and feel, not better cutting.
[thoughtful] And the Singapore catch, because there's always one.
There is. You largely can't carry one here — the law names lawful reasons, and self-defence isn't on the list. So it's a collector's and traveller's thing, not a pocket-carry thing. Enjoy it at home.
[curious] And past the grail — is there a further out there?

There is a custom world — Russian mid-techs, a Canadian maker who sells by lottery for around a thousand dollars. But the honest line is the sceptic's: past the mid-tier, for opening mail, a fifty-dollar steel is genuinely enough. If it isn't cutting, it's jewellery.
[amused] A whole desk about a tool you're not allowed to use. Very us.
One gadget and one watch, quickly. XREAL's Aura — see-through Android glasses, a real Sony micro-display, tethered to a pocket puck by a wire, priced at, quote, no more than fifteen hundred dollars.
[wry] But they won't actually say the price.

Everything but a price. Watch it; don't buy it yet. And Zenith took its famous chronograph movement, the El Primero, and built a watch around it with no chronograph. Time-only. Ten thousand nine hundred dollars.
[laughs] So you pay El Primero money to not use the El Primero.
That is the sceptic's entire case, yes.
[laughs] Okay. Culture, before you take my hand.
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is the fastest film ever to nine hundred million dollars at home — thirty-six days — and past two billion worldwide.
Huge.
Huge, with an asterisk: it's the lowest-reviewed of the run. Event-scale marketing more than fresh storytelling. And Venice hands out its Golden Lion on Saturday — we'll grade our call then.
Anything on the music side?
New releases from Kasabian and Ellie Goulding, and a first American number one for Enhypen — though we flag that chart line as single-sourced until it settles.
The family desk — this one's close to home for our reader.

Singapore's moving on kids and social media. The Prime Minister said self-declaring you're over thirteen is, quote, just not good enough. Mandatory age checks are coming, with a bill in early twenty twenty-seven.
[thoughtful] Does that kind of thing actually work?

Australia's the test case, and it's straining — accounts removed by the million, yet more than eight in ten under-sixteens still online. The honest science says the highest-leverage move isn't a ban. It's the phone out of the bedroom at night.
[warmly] That's the one that protects sleep. Simple, unglamorous, real.
Quick one for the calendar — anything to actually book this week?
One alarm to set. Bruno Mars tickets go on sale Friday the eleventh — four nights in Singapore next April, the easiest family stadium booking of the season.
[warmly] Noted for the household.

And if Japan's on the cards, Kyushu sumo tickets open on the nineteenth, and the good dates vanish within the hour. A sumo tournament is the rare thing a twelve-year-old still talks about years later — pick your day first.
And on fitness — a hard number on lifting. Ninety to a hundred twenty minutes of strength work a week is the sweet spot. After that, the mortality curve flattens.
[gasps] That's less than the internet screams at you.
Much less. And strength plus cardio together is about forty-five per cent lower all-cause mortality than neither. The dose is a ceiling as much as a target.
[laughs] I feel personally forgiven. Alright. Now.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[excited] Gravel cycling! A drop-bar bike built for dirt roads and farm tracks, the space between road and mountain bike. The community calls it the gnarmac.
One bike to do everything. It sold on escape — no cars, no pace-line ego, just you and a quiet gravel road.
[warmly] That's the gateway drug right there. And it exploded — the big American race, Unbound, runs a lottery for about five thousand riders now.
And then the money arrived. The gear ladder runs from a genuinely fun bike at two thousand eight hundred dollars to a custom titanium frame at ten to fourteen thousand.
[laughs] There it is.

The community's own tell is the honest one: a reviewer who's tested hundreds of bikes says you don't need to spend more to have more fun, because off-road erases the smooth conditions where the expensive gear shows up.
[curious] So what does the obsessive actually argue about?
One gear versus two. Tyre width — fifty millimetres is the new normal. And whether gravel has, quote, ungravelled — priced out the come-as-you-are crowd that created it.
[thoughtful] The N-plus-one problem. The right number of bikes is always one more than you own.
And there's a real scene here — Coney Island, the Rail Corridor, the sandy trails on Pulau Ubin. An overnight ride to Ubin is the local ritual.
[warmly] I love that. Okay — bring us down slow. The Undercurrent.
[thoughtful] The Philippines. A word: budol.
Budol. What is it?

It started as the name of a street con — budol-budol — where a charming stranger convinces you a bag is full of cash. Inside, only the edges are real money; the rest is paper cut to look like banknotes.
[curious] A swindle.
A swindle. But Gen Z reclaimed the word. Now, na-budol ako — I got budol'd — means you were sweet-talked into buying something you never planned to, and you enjoyed it.
[pause] So the victim became the narrator.

[thoughtful] That's exactly it. And it's happening on TikTok's live-selling streams — six billion dollars of sales last year in the Philippines. Buyers race to type the word MINE to claim a product before it sells out. They call them mine wars.
[thoughtful] Which is the old con, rebuilt. The charming host, the crowd egging you on, the countdown.
Every element. Except now the buyer pays with real money and says thank you. And young Filipinos are taking on their first credit cards just as the persuasion machine hits peak efficiency.
So the joke is doing the work the bank balance can't.

That's the argument. A country that once warned, beware the budol, now narrates its own surrender to it — and laughing about it together is what makes the next purchase easier. When the Financial Times writes this up in three weeks, remember which desk told you first.
[thoughtful] And it's not harmless, is it? The joke does something.

It's load-bearing. Their older survival habit was tingi — buying shampoo and coffee by the single sachet, matching spending to a daily wage. Budol is the opposite: a way to over-commit gracefully, and laugh about it, while the credit card does the quiet work. One rationed scarcity so a household never over-committed; the other rationalises the loss, and turns it into a punchline everyone can share.
[warmly] That's a good one. Genuinely.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
